question.problem:
Given that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14196548/assets/43ec08d3ac9a00921335912f8e2cf8770397f141b4eebbb4f857fd0be69f7441.svg) 
 evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0,1).$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14196548/assets/398ea92d21b959026a702db0f606915acb31906451a9039925518ca79fa89717.svg)

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14196548/assets/5ea286680d2cec429fe920628617d083f47dd53519c2d40f30115dee45a18bc3.svg)

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(\mathbf x) = \det \left( \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf x) \right)
$$

In our case, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14196548/assets/1488754e319066706880b21fd4642c7b6a75a458770cab254b974b13d35425a2.svg)

First, notice that since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14196548/assets/c92e0f35c58187af3fe961947e6e96f0cd82cf32bb00cfd4f51ca3c742339e0c.svg) we must have

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \ln y, 
\qquad 
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y})=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,1) = 0 \cdot 0 - 1\cdot 1 = -1.
$$
